stories.body: At least 750 people have died and more than 3,000 remain missing after floods and landslides triggered by a glacier collapse near the Nepal-China border. Search teams are trying to reach workers missing at hydropower sites and tunnels in Nepal's Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, but heavy rain, rising water and a debris-dammed lake have complicated operations. Nepal says it has mobilized 19,000 security personnel and 16 helicopters, while Chinese authorities are monitoring the remaining risk from the barrier lake with satellites, radar and drones.
stories.headline: Nepal-Tibet floods kill at least 750 as thousands remain missing and rescue efforts face renewed danger

stories.body: Icelanders voted against resuming European Union accession negotiations, with about 52.5% to 52.8% voting no and roughly 47% voting yes. The result leaves the country closely tied to the EU through the single market and Schengen area but without a new push toward membership. Fishing rights, agriculture and concerns about sovereignty dominated the debate, while supporters had argued that membership could offer economic and security benefits amid wider geopolitical uncertainty.
stories.headline: Iceland votes against reopening talks on joining the European Union

stories.body: Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, said a proposed 25-year agreement involving 65 billion barrels of oil would preserve the country's ownership and sovereignty over its resources while bringing in foreign capital, technology and expertise. She said the plan would develop 17 oilfields and eight new blocks, with Venezuela receiving $19 from every barrel sold to the United States. Critics in Venezuela's opposition have condemned reported arrangements for a large US stake in the country's oil and gasfields as unconstitutional and predatory.
stories.headline: Venezuela defends oil agreement with the United States while insisting it retains sovereignty

stories.body: Six months into the Iran war, disruptions in the Gulf and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz have helped push Brent crude from about $72 to $88 a barrel while putting energy infrastructure and long-term investment at risk. Higher prices have boosted oil-company profits, but firms with significant operations in Qatar and the United Arab Emirates have suffered lower output and delayed projects. Analysts say the conflict appears likely to remain a prolonged war of attrition, leaving Gulf economies exposed to continuing supply disruptions and security uncertainty.
stories.headline: Iran war strikes on Gulf energy infrastructure raise new questions for oil markets

stories.body: Niger's ruling junta said it had regained control after mutinying soldiers fired on sensitive sites and attempted to storm the presidential palace in Niamey. Gunfire and explosions were reported for hours in what officials described as a serious challenge to the military government. Security forces were deployed around key locations, including the airport, although reports indicated the situation had not yet fully stabilized.
stories.headline: Niger junta says it has regained control after soldiers mutiny in Niamey

stories.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping are due to attend a two-day summit in Kyrgyzstan alongside the leaders of Iran and India. The gathering is intended to project unity among the participating countries as Russia's war in Ukraine, the conflict involving Iran and broader tensions with Western powers continue to reshape regional politics.
stories.headline: Putin and Xi prepare for Central Asia summit aimed at countering Western influence

stories.body: Columbia, South Carolina, police officer Christopher DeLong, 29, was killed and another officer, David Dymock, was injured in a gunfight at a park after police responded to a domestic-dispute call. Police said the suspected shooter, a 33-year-old man with a lengthy criminal record, was also killed. Dymock was reported to be in stable condition, while DeLong, who had served with the department for two years, is survived by his wife and two young children.
stories.headline: Police officer killed and another injured in shooting at a South Carolina park

stories.body: A federal judge in California ruled that the US government cannot deport noncitizens solely for speech criticizing Israel or supporting Palestinians, finding that parts of the administration's approach violated First and Fifth Amendment protections. The decision was a victory for The Stanford Daily, whose international-student journalists said deportation threats had chilled speech. Judge Noël Wise said free expression cannot be limited to views that flatter the government and warned that retaliation for disfavored opinions is incompatible with constitutional protections.
stories.headline: Judge rules Trump administration cannot deport students solely for criticizing Israel

stories.body: Six months into the Iran war, the economic effects in the United States have been uneven: rising energy prices have benefited some investors and energy producers while increasing costs for consumers and straining sectors exposed to higher fuel prices and disrupted international travel. Early forecasts of broad economic catastrophe have not fully materialized, but the conflict's effect on oil markets and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continues to create uncertainty for businesses and households.
stories.headline: Iran war produces an uneven economic toll for US consumers, businesses and investors

stories.body: Spain's government is expected to approve a €165 million emergency plan for Ceuta aimed at supporting the local economy and strengthening public services after the mass arrival of migrants from Morocco. The package includes aid for small businesses, self-employed workers, commerce, tourism, education, health care and justice, and comes alongside previously announced funding for migrant children, humanitarian assistance and a longer-term recovery plan. Around 5,000 migrants were still reported to be in the autonomous city a month after the arrivals.
stories.headline: Spain announces a €165 million emergency plan as the Ceuta migration crisis continues

stories.body: A month after tens of thousands of migrants entered Ceuta from Morocco, thousands remain in the small autonomous city and residents describe deep anxiety, frustration and a sense of institutional abandonment. The crisis has fueled protests and sharpened political pressure on Spain's government, while local officials and residents fear that strained public services, insecurity concerns and unmet expectations over returns could damage Ceuta's long-standing multicultural coexistence.
stories.headline: Ceuta tensions persist a month after mass migrant arrivals, amid protests and mounting political pressure

stories.body: Reports from Ceuta describe a sharp rise in online hate speech and disinformation following the mass migrant arrivals, with an observatory identifying 9,590 hateful posts in the first 48 hours of the crisis. Much of the rhetoric dehumanized North African migrants, and researchers warn that such narratives can normalize discrimination and violence. The tense online climate has been reflected on the ground in protests, attacks on migrant encampments and intimidation, while aid groups continue to assist people without adequate shelter.
stories.headline: Online disinformation and dehumanizing rhetoric intensify the Ceuta migration crisis

stories.body: Morocco has renewed assertions of a historic claim over the Spanish autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla as the migration crisis continues to strain relations with Madrid. Moroccan officials have called for the return of unaccompanied Moroccan minors and have linked the issue to broader sovereignty claims, while Spain has emphasized that returns must follow legal procedures. The dispute adds diplomatic and political pressure to a crisis in which many migrants remain in Ceuta and numerous people died during the mass crossings.
stories.headline: Morocco renews its claim over Ceuta and Melilla amid the migration crisis

stories.body: High-speed rail traffic between Barcelona and Girona was suspended after a loss of electrical power in the overhead line near La Sagrera. The outage affected all operators and left an Avant service to Figueres and an AVE train bound for Lyon disrupted; passengers on the Avant were evacuated, while the Lyon service returned to Sants. Civil Protection activated a pre-alert, Adif began repairs, and Renfe redirected passengers to conventional regional services while there was no timetable for restoring high-speed operations.
stories.headline: High-speed rail service between Barcelona and Girona is suspended after an electrical failure near La Sagrera

stories.body: Barcelona Mayor Jaume Collboni will visit Kyiv on September 3 and 4 with the city's fire chief, Sebastià Massagué, where Barcelona plans to provide additional fire and emergency vehicles to Ukraine's state emergency service. Collboni is expected to meet Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko as part of an eastern European trip that also includes Sarajevo and Warsaw. Catalan President Salvador Illa is also expected to travel to Kyiv, with both leaders presenting the visits as expressions of solidarity with Ukraine and Barcelona's role as a city of peace.
stories.headline: Barcelona mayor Jaume Collboni plans Kyiv visit and further emergency-vehicle aid for Ukraine
